Generalized Wasserstein Distances

This chapter keeps the idea of comparing measures while changing the geometry of the comparison. The constructions below relax mass conservation, average lower-dimensional projections, quotient nuisance symmetries, linearize transport around a reference measure, replace the trace cost by spectral gauges, or constrain motion to conditional fibers. They are useful when standard Wp\Wass_pWp​ is too rigid or too expensive, but each modification also changes which metric, geodesic, or stability properties survive.

Guiding Comparison

Balanced Wasserstein fixes the marginals exactly. Unbalanced OT relaxes the marginals. Sliced OT compares many one-dimensional shadows. Linear OT embeds measures through maps from a fixed reference. Spectral OT changes the scalar quadratic cost into a gauge of the whole displacement covariance. Quotient OT removes prescribed symmetries, while conditional OT prohibits transport across different fibers.

Unbalanced OT¶

Unbalanced OT allows mass creation and destruction by penalizing marginal mismatch. It is essential when histograms are not normalized, when observations contain outliers, or when only part of the source should match the target Liero et al., 2018Chizat et al., 2018Chizat et al., 2018.

Relaxed Formulation¶

For nonnegative measures (α,β)∈M+(X)×M+(Y)(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal M_+(\X)\times\mathcal M_+(\Y)(α,β)∈M+​(X)×M+​(Y), a generic relaxed formulation is

UWc(α,β)=inf⁡π∈M+(X×Y)∫X×Yc(x,y) dπ(x,y)+Dψ1(π1∣α)+Dψ2(π2∣β),\mathsf{UW}_c(\alpha,\beta) = \inf_{\pi\in\mathcal M_+(\X\times\Y)} \int_{\X\times\Y} c(x,y)\d\pi(x,y) + \mathcal D_{\psi_1}(\pi_1\mid\alpha) + \mathcal D_{\psi_2}(\pi_2\mid\beta),UWc​(α,β)=π∈M+​(X×Y)inf​∫X×Y​c(x,y)dπ(x,y)+Dψ1​​(π1​∣α)+Dψ2​​(π2​∣β),
(1)

where ψ1,ψ2\psi_1,\psi_2ψ1​,ψ2​ are convex entropy functions. Exact conservation (π1,π2)=(α,β)(\pi_1,\pi_2)=(\alpha,\beta)(π1​,π2​)=(α,β) is replaced by a cost for changing the marginals. Writing ψs=τψˉs\psi_s=\tau\bar\psi_sψs​=τψˉ​s​ exposes the relaxation scale:

UWc,τ(α,β)=inf⁡π≥0∫c dπ+τDψˉ1(π1∣α)+τDψˉ2(π2∣β).\mathsf{UW}_{c,\tau}(\alpha,\beta) = \inf_{\pi\geq0} \int c\d\pi + \tau\mathcal D_{\bar\psi_1}(\pi_1\mid\alpha) + \tau\mathcal D_{\bar\psi_2}(\pi_2\mid\beta).UWc,τ​(α,β)=π≥0inf​∫cdπ+τDψˉ​1​​(π1​∣α)+τDψˉ​2​​(π2​∣β).
(2)

Large τ\tauτ makes marginal mismatch expensive and approaches balanced OT when the total masses are compatible. Small τ\tauτ makes creation and destruction cheap; after rescaling by τ\tauτ, the zero-transport part reveals the pure divergence geometry.

The two immediate numerical displays make the penalty roles explicit. Div fixes a KL marginal penalty and varies τ\tauτ: the transported marginals, shown in violet, are allowed to differ from the prescribed red and blue marginals, and the gaps are precisely the created or destroyed mass. Div then keeps the geometry, entropic plan regularization and relaxation strength fixed, and changes only the marginal divergence. This isolates the effect of the penalty: KL gives smooth rescaling, Burg discourages complete deletion of prescribed modes, while total variation produces sharper active-mass selection.

show_book_figure("unbalanced-mass-relaxation")

KL unbalanced OT on one-dimensional Gaussian-mixture densities. The central matrix is the transported coupling. The side curves compare the prescribed marginals with the transported marginals; increasing τ\tauτ makes marginal mismatch more expensive, so more mass is moved rather than created or destroyed.

The entropy used in the marginal relaxation also changes the qualitative behavior. A KL penalty leads to smooth multiplicative rescaling. The reverse-KL, or Burg, penalty blows up when a transported marginal vanishes where the prescribed marginal is positive, so it discourages complete deletion of small modes. Total variation has a linear kink and behaves closer to partial transport: mass is either kept active or created and destroyed at nearly constant marginal price.

show_book_figure("unbalanced-divergence-choice")

Effect of the marginal divergence in unbalanced entropic OT. The geometric cost, entropic plan regularization ϵ\epsilonϵ, and relaxation strength τ\tauτ are fixed; only the marginal penalty changes. KL allows smooth mass variation, Burg keeps transported marginals from vanishing on prescribed modes, and total variation gives a sharper active-mass selection.

Interactive panel. Use the middle-τ\tauτ, ϵ\epsilonϵ, and grid controls to compare KL unbalanced couplings for the same source and target marginals as in the book figure.

These figures should be read as pictures of a single relaxed plan π\piπ: the same nonnegative measure determines both the transported coupling and its two relaxed marginals. The small-τ\tauτ result below formalizes the opposite regime, where transport becomes negligible compared with local mass variation.

Reverse and Homogeneous Formulations¶

The Liero--Mielke--Savare formulation rewrites marginal penalties as a local transport cost and then homogenizes it. Assuming first that the reference measures and transported marginals have mutually absolutely continuous parts, one can factor the objective as

∫c(x,y) dπ(x,y)+Dψ1(π1∣α)+Dψ2(π2∣β)=∫(c(x,y)+ψ1 ⁣( dπ1 dα(x)) dα dπ1(x)+ψ2 ⁣( dπ2 dβ(y)) dβ dπ2(y)) dπ(x,y).\begin{aligned} &\int c(x,y)\d\pi(x,y) + \mathcal D_{\psi_1}(\pi_1\mid\alpha) + \mathcal D_{\psi_2}(\pi_2\mid\beta) \\ &\quad = \int \left( c(x,y) + \psi_1\!\left(\frac{\d\pi_1}{\d\alpha}(x)\right) \frac{\d\alpha}{\d\pi_1}(x) + \psi_2\!\left(\frac{\d\pi_2}{\d\beta}(y)\right) \frac{\d\beta}{\d\pi_2}(y) \right) \d\pi(x,y). \end{aligned}​∫c(x,y)dπ(x,y)+Dψ1​​(π1​∣α)+Dψ2​​(π2​∣β)=∫(c(x,y)+ψ1​(dαdπ1​​(x))dπ1​dα​(x)+ψ2​(dβdπ2​​(y))dπ2​dβ​(y))dπ(x,y).​
(10)

This motivates the local reverse cost

Lc(r,s):=c+rψ1(1/r)+sψ2(1/s),L_c(r,s) \eqdef c+r\psi_1(1/r)+s\psi_2(1/s),Lc​(r,s):=c+rψ1​(1/r)+sψ2​(1/s),
(11)

with the usual recession convention at r=0r=0r=0 or s=0s=0s=0. If α=Fπ1+α⊥\alpha=F\pi_1+\alpha^\perpα=Fπ1​+α⊥ and β=Gπ2+β⊥\beta=G\pi_2+\beta^\perpβ=Gπ2​+β⊥ are the Lebesgue decompositions of the reference marginals with respect to the transported marginals, then

UWc(α,β)=inf⁡π≥0∫Lc(x,y)(F(x),G(y)) dπ(x,y)+ψ1(0)α⊥(X)+ψ2(0)β⊥(Y).\mathsf{UW}_c(\alpha,\beta) = \inf_{\pi\geq0} \int L_{c(x,y)}(F(x),G(y))\d\pi(x,y) + \psi_1(0)\alpha^\perp(\X) + \psi_2(0)\beta^\perp(\Y).UWc​(α,β)=π≥0inf​∫Lc(x,y)​(F(x),G(y))dπ(x,y)+ψ1​(0)α⊥(X)+ψ2​(0)β⊥(Y).
(12)

The homogeneous formulation is obtained by taking the perspective transform of LcL_cLc​,

Hc(r,s):=inf⁡θ>0θLc(r/θ,s/θ),H_c(r,s) \eqdef \inf_{\theta>0} \theta L_c(r/\theta,s/\theta),Hc​(r,s):=θ>0inf​θLc​(r/θ,s/θ),
(13)

which is positively 1-homogeneous. It defines

HWc(α,β)=inf⁡π≥0∫Hc(x,y)(F(x),G(y)) dπ(x,y)+ψ1(0)α⊥(X)+ψ2(0)β⊥(Y).\mathsf{HW}_c(\alpha,\beta) = \inf_{\pi\geq0} \int H_{c(x,y)}(F(x),G(y))\d\pi(x,y) + \psi_1(0)\alpha^\perp(\X) + \psi_2(0)\beta^\perp(\Y).HWc​(α,β)=π≥0inf​∫Hc(x,y)​(F(x),G(y))dπ(x,y)+ψ1​(0)α⊥(X)+ψ2​(0)β⊥(Y).
(14)

For both the proof and the cone construction, it is useful to expose the equivalent semi-coupling form Liero et al., 2018:

HWc(α,β)=inf⁡λ∈M+(X×Y)u,v≥0{∫Hc(x,y)(u(x,y),v(x,y)) dλ(x,y)  ;  (p1)♯(uλ)=α,(p2)♯(vλ)=β}.\mathsf{HW}_c(\alpha,\beta) = \inf_{\substack{\lambda\in\mathcal M_+(\X\times\Y)\\u,v\geq0}} \left\{ \int H_{c(x,y)}(u(x,y),v(x,y))\d\lambda(x,y) \; ;\; (\mathrm p_1)_\sharp(u\lambda)=\alpha,\quad (\mathrm p_2)_\sharp(v\lambda)=\beta \right\}.HWc​(α,β)=λ∈M+​(X×Y)u,v≥0​inf​{∫Hc(x,y)​(u(x,y),v(x,y))dλ(x,y);(p1​)♯​(uλ)=α,(p2​)♯​(vλ)=β}.
(15)

Proposition: Homogenization Does Not Change the Cost

Assume that the entropy functions are proper, lower semicontinuous and convex, with their usual recession extensions at zero. Then

HWc(α,β)=UWc(α,β).\mathsf{HW}_c(\alpha,\beta)=\mathsf{UW}_c(\alpha,\beta).HWc​(α,β)=UWc​(α,β).

Theorem: Cone Formulation of Unbalanced OT

Assume that X\XX is compact, that (r,s)↦Hc(x,y)(r,s)(r,s)\mapsto H_{c(x,y)}(r,s)(r,s)↦Hc(x,y)​(r,s) is convex for every (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), and that (x,y,r,s)↦Hc(x,y)(r,s)(x,y,r,s)\mapsto H_{c(x,y)}(r,s)(x,y,r,s)↦Hc(x,y)​(r,s) is lower semicontinuous. Then UWc=HWc=CW\mathsf{UW}_c=\mathsf{HW}_c=\mathsf{CW}UWc​=HWc​=CW. If, in addition, D\mathsf DD is a continuous distance on the cone, then CW1/p\mathsf{CW}^{1/p}CW1/p is a distance between nonnegative finite measures.

Proof

The equality UW=HW\mathsf{UW}=\mathsf{HW}UW=HW is the preceding proposition. A feasible semi-coupling (λ,u,v)(\lambda,u,v)(λ,u,v) lifts to the cone through

(x,y)⟼((x,u(x,y)1/p),(y,v(x,y)1/p)).(x,y)\longmapsto \big((x,u(x,y)^{1/p}),(y,v(x,y)^{1/p})\big).(x,y)⟼((x,u(x,y)1/p),(y,v(x,y)1/p)).
(25)

Its weighted base marginals are α,β\alpha,\betaα,β, and its cone action is exactly ∫Hc(x,y)(u,v) dλ\int H_{c(x,y)}(u,v)\d\lambda∫Hc(x,y)​(u,v)dλ, so CW≤HW\mathsf{CW}\leq\mathsf{HW}CW≤HW. Conversely, disintegrate a cone plan over (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) and set u=E[rp∣x,y]u=\mathbb E[r^p\mid x,y]u=E[rp∣x,y] and v=E[sp∣x,y]v=\mathbb E[s^p\mid x,y]v=E[sp∣x,y]. Jensen’s inequality for the convex function HcH_cHc​ produces a feasible semi-coupling of no larger action. Hence HW≤CW\mathsf{HW}\leq\mathsf{CW}HW≤CW.

For the triangle inequality, two plans that share the same weighted middle projection need not share the same ordinary cone marginal. Homogeneity is the essential correction: common radial rescaling preserves weighted projections and action. After normalization and addition of harmless apex mass, two nearly optimal plans for (α,β)(\alpha,\beta)(α,β) and (β,ζ)(\beta,\zeta)(β,ζ) can be given the same ordinary middle lift

Mδo+(x↦(x,1))♯βM\delta_{\mathfrak o}+(x\mapsto(x,1))_\sharp\betaMδo​+(x↦(x,1))♯​β
(26)

for a sufficiently large finite MMM. The ordinary gluing lemma and Minkowski’s inequality then prove the triangle inequality. Radial normalization by (rp+sp)1/p(r^p+s^p)^{1/p}(rp+sp)1/p also restricts minimizing plans to bounded radii and fixed mass; compactness and lower semicontinuity yield an optimizer. A zero-action optimizer is concentrated on the cone diagonal, so its two weighted projections coincide and α=β\alpha=\betaα=β.

A generic entropic regularization of unbalanced OT reads

f←ω gcˉ,ϵ,g←ω fc,ϵ,ω:=ττ+ϵ,f\leftarrow\omega\,g^{\bar c,\epsilon}, \qquad g\leftarrow\omega\,f^{c,\epsilon}, \qquad \omega\eqdef\frac{\tau}{\tau+\epsilon},f←ωgcˉ,ϵ,g←ωfc,ϵ,ω:=τ+ϵτ​,

f(x)=−τϵτ+ϵlog⁡∫Yexp⁡(g(y)−c(x,y)ϵ) dβ(y),g(y)=−τϵτ+ϵlog⁡∫Xexp⁡(f(x)−c(x,y)ϵ) dα(x).\begin{aligned} f(x) &= - \frac{\tau\epsilon}{\tau+\epsilon} \log\int_\Y \exp\left(\frac{g(y)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon}\right)\d\beta(y),\\ g(y) &= - \frac{\tau\epsilon}{\tau+\epsilon} \log\int_\X \exp\left(\frac{f(x)-c(x,y)}{\epsilon}\right)\d\alpha(x). \end{aligned}f(x)g(y)​=−τ+ϵτϵ​log∫Y​exp(ϵg(y)−c(x,y)​)dβ(y),=−τ+ϵτϵ​log∫X​exp(ϵf(x)−c(x,y)​)dα(x).​

In the discrete case, with Ki,j=e−Ci,j/ϵaibjK_{i,j}=e^{-C_{i,j}/\epsilon}a_i b_jKi,j​=e−Ci,j​/ϵai​bj​ and ω=τ/(τ+ϵ)\omega=\tau/(\tau+\epsilon)ω=τ/(τ+ϵ), this gives the generalized Sinkhorn scaling

ui←(ai(Kv)i)ω,vj←(bj(K⊤u)j)ω,P=diag⁡(u)Kdiag⁡(v).u_i\leftarrow \left(\frac{a_i}{(Kv)_i}\right)^\omega, \qquad v_j\leftarrow \left(\frac{b_j}{(K^\top u)_j}\right)^\omega, \qquad P=\diag(u)K\diag(v).ui​←((Kv)i​ai​​)ω,vj​←((K⊤u)j​bj​​)ω,P=diag(u)Kdiag(v).

The exponent ω<1\omega<1ω<1 is the visible difference with balanced Sinkhorn: marginal corrections are damped because violating the marginals is allowed.

The KL case in Div is obtained from these damped updates. The interactive panel above exposes the two most important regularization scales. Increasing τ\tauτ pushes the transported marginals closer to the prescribed ones; increasing ϵ\epsilonϵ spreads the coupling itself.

Metric Contraction of the Damped Updates¶

Balanced entropic potentials have a gauge ambiguity, whereas KL marginal penalties make the unbalanced potentials unique up to null sets. The natural metric is therefore the ordinary L∞L^\inftyL∞ distance on potentials, or, equivalently, the Thompson metric on positive scalings,

dT((u,v),(u′,v′)):=max⁡{∥log⁡u−log⁡u′∥∞,∥log⁡v−log⁡v′∥∞}.d_T((u,v),(u',v')) \eqdef \max\{\|\log u-\log u'\|_\infty, \|\log v-\log v'\|_\infty\}.dT​((u,v),(u′,v′)):=max{∥logu−logu′∥∞​,∥logv−logv′∥∞​}.
(32)
Proposition: Linear Contraction of Unbalanced Sinkhorn

Assume that the damped soft-transform map sends bounded potentials to bounded potentials, as happens when ccc is bounded. With ω=τ/(τ+ϵ)<1\omega=\tau/(\tau+\epsilon)<1ω=τ/(τ+ϵ)<1, define

TGS(f,g)=(f~,g~),f~=ωgcˉ,ϵ,g~=ωf~c,ϵ.\mathcal T_{\rm GS}(f,g)=(\widetilde f,\widetilde g), \qquad \widetilde f=\omega g^{\bar c,\epsilon}, \qquad \widetilde g=\omega\widetilde f^{c,\epsilon}.TGS​(f,g)=(f​,g​),f​=ωgcˉ,ϵ,g​=ωf​c,ϵ.
(33)

Then, for d∞((f,g),(f′,g′))=max⁡{∥f−f′∥∞,∥g−g′∥∞}d_\infty((f,g),(f',g'))=\max\{\|f-f'\|_\infty,\|g-g'\|_\infty\}d∞​((f,g),(f′,g′))=max{∥f−f′∥∞​,∥g−g′∥∞​},

d∞(TGS(f,g),TGS(f′,g′))≤ωd∞((f,g),(f′,g′)).d_\infty(\mathcal T_{\rm GS}(f,g),\mathcal T_{\rm GS}(f',g')) \leq \omega d_\infty((f,g),(f',g')).d∞​(TGS​(f,g),TGS​(f′,g′))≤ωd∞​((f,g),(f′,g′)).
(34)

Consequently the bounded fixed point is unique and both the potential distance and the Thompson distance of the scalings decay at least as ωk\omega^kωk.

Proof

Soft ccc-transforms are order reversing, commute with additive constants up to sign, and are 1-Lipschitz in L∞L^\inftyL∞. Thus, writing D=d∞((f,g),(f′,g′))D=d_\infty((f,g),(f',g'))D=d∞​((f,g),(f′,g′)),

∥f~−f~′∥∞≤ωD,∥g~−g~′∥∞≤ω∥f~−f~′∥∞≤ω2D.\|\widetilde f-\widetilde f'\|_\infty\leq\omega D, \qquad \|\widetilde g-\widetilde g'\|_\infty \leq\omega\|\widetilde f-\widetilde f'\|_\infty \leq\omega^2D.∥f​−f​′∥∞​≤ωD,∥g​−g​′∥∞​≤ω∥f​−f​′∥∞​≤ω2D.
(35)

Hence the product distance contracts by ω\omegaω. Banach’s fixed-point theorem gives existence, uniqueness, and the geometric rate.

Algorithm: Unbalanced Sinkhorn scaling

Output: Unbalanced entropic coupling P\PP.

Initialize: Set Kij=e−Cij/ϵaibj,ω=ττ+ϵ,u(0)=1n,v(0)=1m,η0=+∞,k=0.K_{ij}=e^{-\C_{ij}/\epsilon}\a_i\b_j, \quad \omega=\frac{\tau}{\tau+\epsilon}, \quad u^{(0)}=\ones_n, \quad v^{(0)}=\ones_m, \quad \eta_0=+\infty, \quad k=0.Kij​=e−Cij​/ϵai​bj​,ω=τ+ϵτ​,u(0)=1n​,v(0)=1m​,η0​=+∞,k=0.

Partial Optimal Transport¶

Total variation gives a sharp active-mass selection and connects unbalanced OT with the classical partial-transport problem. The latter fixes in advance the amount of transported mass. For

0≤m≤min⁡{α(X),β(Y)},0\leq m\leq \min\{\alpha(\X),\beta(\Y)\},0≤m≤min{α(X),β(Y)},
(36)

define

POT⁡m(α,β):=inf⁡π∈M+(X×Y)π1≤α, π2≤βπ(X×Y)=m∫c  dπ.\operatorname{POT}_m(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \inf_{\substack{\pi\in\mathcal M_+(\X\times\Y)\\ \pi_1\leq\alpha,\ \pi_2\leq\beta\\ \pi(\X\times\Y)=m}} \int c\,\d\pi .POTm​(α,β):=π∈M+​(X×Y)π1​≤α, π2​≤βπ(X×Y)=m​inf​∫cdπ.
(37)

Thus only a submeasure of α\alphaα is transported onto a submeasure of β\betaβ; the remaining mass is left unmatched. The corresponding Lagrangian form is obtained by adding total-variation penalties. For a price λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 for discarding or creating one unit of mass, denote by POT⁡λTV(α,β)\operatorname{POT}^{\TV}_\lambda(\alpha,\beta)POTλTV​(α,β) the value

inf⁡π∈M+(X×Y)∫c  dπ+λ∥α−π1∥TV+λ∥β−π2∥TV.\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal M_+(\X\times\Y)} \int c\,\d\pi + \lambda\|\alpha-\pi_1\|_{\TV} + \lambda\|\beta-\pi_2\|_{\TV}.π∈M+​(X×Y)inf​∫cdπ+λ∥α−π1​∥TV​+λ∥β−π2​∥TV​.
(38)

Assume c≥0c\geq0c≥0. Allowing transported marginals larger than the available marginals does not improve the value: excess transported mass can be trimmed, which decreases the transport cost and cannot increase the sum of the two total-variation penalties. Hence an optimal plan may be chosen with π1≤α\pi_1\leq\alphaπ1​≤α and π2≤β\pi_2\leq\betaπ2​≤β. If m=π(X×Y)m=\pi(\X\times\Y)m=π(X×Y), the penalty then reduces to

λ(α(X)−m)+λ(β(Y)−m),\lambda\big(\alpha(\X)-m\big)+\lambda\big(\beta(\Y)-m\big),λ(α(X)−m)+λ(β(Y)−m),
(39)

so the precise relation is a one-dimensional Lagrange duality in the transported mass.

Proposition: TV Penalization Selects Fixed-Mass Partial OT

Assume that X,Y\X,\YX,Y are compact metric spaces and that ccc is continuous and nonnegative. Set A=α(X)A=\alpha(\X)A=α(X), B=β(Y)B=\beta(\Y)B=β(Y), and M=min⁡(A,B)M=\min(A,B)M=min(A,B). Then

POT⁡λTV(α,β)=λ(A+B)+inf⁡0≤m≤M{POT⁡m(α,β)−2λm}.\operatorname{POT}^{\TV}_\lambda(\alpha,\beta) = \lambda(A+B) + \inf_{0\leq m\leq M} \big\{\operatorname{POT}_m(\alpha,\beta)-2\lambda m\big\}.POTλTV​(α,β)=λ(A+B)+0≤m≤Minf​{POTm​(α,β)−2λm}.
(40)

If a penalized optimizer has mass mλm_\lambdamλ​, it is optimal for POT⁡mλ\operatorname{POT}_{m_\lambda}POTmλ​​ and mλm_\lambdamλ​ minimizes the scalar problem. Conversely, if 2λ∈∂POT⁡m2\lambda\in\partial\operatorname{POT}_m2λ∈∂POTm​, every fixed-mass optimizer is penalized-optimal. Every m∈[0,M]m\in[0,M]m∈[0,M] is selected by at least one λ≥0\lambda\geq0λ≥0, possibly together with an interval of masses on a flat exposed face.

Proof

Write V(m)=POT⁡m(α,β)V(m)=\operatorname{POT}_m(\alpha,\beta)V(m)=POTm​(α,β). Compactness gives an optimizer. Convex combinations of subcouplings show that VVV is convex, while rescaling a plan shows that it is nondecreasing. If m0<m1m_0<m_1m0​<m1​, choose submeasures of mass m1−m0m_1-m_0m1​−m0​ from the residual source and target measures of an optimizer at m0m_0m0​, couple them, and add this coupling. This proves V(m1)−V(m0)≤∥c∥∞(m1−m0)V(m_1)-V(m_0)\leq\|c\|_\infty(m_1-m_0)V(m1​)−V(m0​)≤∥c∥∞​(m1​−m0​), so VVV is Lipschitz.

Grouping every penalized competitor by its total transported mass gives the displayed scalar infimum. Equality forces simultaneous optimality in the fixed-mass and scalar problems. The converse is precisely the subgradient inequality. Since the extended convex function is Lipschitz on [0,M][0,M][0,M] and nondecreasing, a nonnegative subgradient exists at every mass after including the interval’s normal cone.

Proposition: Fixed Total Mass Reduces Partial OT to Balanced OT

Let c=dpc=d^pc=dp, p≥1p\geq1p≥1, and fix m>0m>0m>0. On nonnegative measures of total mass exactly mmm and finite pppth moment,

POT⁡m(α,β)1/p=m1/pWp(α/m,β/m)\operatorname{POT}_m(\alpha,\beta)^{1/p} = m^{1/p}\Wass_p(\alpha/m,\beta/m)POTm​(α,β)1/p=m1/pWp​(α/m,β/m)
(41)

is a distance. On the larger class of measures with mass at least mmm, it is not a distance in general.

Proof

When both endpoint masses equal mmm, the inequalities π1≤α\pi_1\leq\alphaπ1​≤α, π2≤β\pi_2\leq\betaπ2​≤β and the mass constraint force π1=α\pi_1=\alphaπ1​=α, π2=β\pi_2=\betaπ2​=β. Thus partial couplings are exactly balanced couplings, and normalization by mmm gives the formula. On a larger class, α=mδx+rδy\alpha=m\delta_x+r\delta_yα=mδx​+rδy​ and β=mδx+rδz\beta=m\delta_x+r\delta_zβ=mδx​+rδz​ are distinct but share the zero-cost partial plan mδ(x,x)m\delta_{(x,x)}mδ(x,x)​.

Thus TV penalization is the Lagrangian envelope of constrained partial OT: increasing λ\lambdaλ selects larger transported masses, while small λ\lambdaλ makes deletion and creation cheaper. The constrained theory, including active regions and free boundaries, was developed by Caffarelli--McCann and Figalli Caffarelli & McCann (2010)Figalli (2010). Modern computational and learning applications include partial Wasserstein and partial Gromov--Wasserstein variants, for instance in Chapel--Alaya--Gasso Chapel et al. (2020).

Example: Application to proliferating and dying cell populations

In single-cell time courses, the observed populations can grow, die or change composition between two sampling times. A balanced coupling would force every unit of mass at time ttt to reappear at time t+Δtt+\Delta tt+Δt, which is too rigid biologically. The relaxed value

inf⁡π≥0∫c dπ+τ1D(π1∣αt)+τ2D(π2∣αt+Δt)\inf_{\pi\geq0}\int c\d\pi +\tau_1\Dd(\pi_1|\al_t) +\tau_2\Dd(\pi_2|\al_{t+\Delta t})π≥0inf​∫cdπ+τ1​D(π1​∣αt​)+τ2​D(π2​∣αt+Δt​)
(42)

where π1,π2\pi_1,\pi_2π1​,π2​ are the marginals of π\piπ, interprets missing marginal mass as death or undersampling, and excess target marginal mass as growth or birth. Neural semi-coupling and entropic dynamic variants use this idea to model proliferating or dying cell populations from unpaired measurements Lübeck et al., 2022Klein et al., 2023. The dynamic counterpart, where creation and transport are both part of the tangent dynamics, is discussed in Section Dynamic Unbalanced OT and WFR Flows.

Sliced Wasserstein Distances¶

Sliced Wasserstein distances replace one high-dimensional comparison by an average of explicit one-dimensional optimal transport problems.

One-Dimensional Projections¶

The idea was proposed by Marc Bernot, and its first published use for Wasserstein barycenters and texture mixing is due to Rabin, Peyré, Delon and Bernot Rabin et al., 2011. It is cheap, differentiable after sorting, and often effective in imaging and learning. For measures on Rd\RR^dRd and θ∈Sd−1\theta\in\mathbb S^{d-1}θ∈Sd−1, let Pθ(x)=⟨θ,x⟩P_\theta(x)=\dotp{\theta}{x}Pθ​(x)=⟨θ,x⟩.

Spherical Averaging¶

The projected measures live on the real line, where Wasserstein distances are explicit through sorting or quantiles. Averaging over directions defines the sliced distance.

Definition: Sliced Wasserstein Distance

Let p≥1p\geq1p≥1, let α,β∈Pp(Rd)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal P_p(\RR^d)α,β∈Pp​(Rd), and let σ\sigmaσ be the uniform probability measure on Sd−1\mathbb S^{d-1}Sd−1. The sliced ppp-Wasserstein distance is

SW⁡p(α,β)p:=∫Sd−1Wp((Pθ)♯α,(Pθ)♯β)p dσ(θ).\operatorname{SW}_p(\alpha,\beta)^p \eqdef \int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}} \Wass_p\big((P_\theta)_\sharp\alpha,(P_\theta)_\sharp\beta\big)^p \d\sigma(\theta).SWp​(α,β)p:=∫Sd−1​Wp​((Pθ​)♯​α,(Pθ​)♯​β)pdσ(θ).
(43)

Since each projected problem can be solved by sorting or quantiles, SW⁡p\operatorname{SW}_pSWp​ is much cheaper to approximate numerically than high-dimensional OT. It metrizes the same weak-plus-moment topology as Wp\Wass_pWp​, but its geometry is not bi-Lipschitz equivalent to Wp\Wass_pWp​ in high dimension Nadjahi et al., 2019.

Remark: Radon viewpoint

Slicing can also be understood as applying a Radon transform before measuring discrepancy. For a probability measure α\alα on Rd\RR^dRd, define its measure-valued Radon transform by

Rα(θ):=(Pθ)♯α,θ∈Sd−1.\mathfrak R\al(\theta)\eqdef (P_\theta)_\sharp\al, \qquad \theta\in\Sphere^{d-1}.Rα(θ):=(Pθ​)♯​α,θ∈Sd−1.
(44)

Thus Rα\mathfrak R\alRα is a collection of one-dimensional projected measures indexed by directions. If α=ρ(x) dx\al=\rho(x)\d xα=ρ(x)dx has a density, then Rα(θ)\mathfrak R\al(\theta)Rα(θ) has density given by the classical Radon transform

Rρ(θ,s)=∫{x:⟨θ,x⟩=s}ρ(x)  dHd−1(x).R\rho(\theta,s) = \int_{\{x:\dotp{\theta}{x}=s\}}\rho(x)\,\d\mathcal H^{d-1}(x).Rρ(θ,s)=∫{x:⟨θ,x⟩=s}​ρ(x)dHd−1(x).
(45)

With this notation, (43) says that SW⁡p\SW_pSWp​ is the pull-back, through R\mathfrak RR, of the Lp(Sd−1;Wp)L^p(\Sphere^{d-1};\Wass_p)Lp(Sd−1;Wp​) distance on Radon data. The full all-direction transform is injective on probability measures by the Cramer--Wold theorem, which is why sliced Wasserstein separates measures. The warning is numerical and variational: finitely sampled Radon data are not injective, and independently constructed one-dimensional Radon data need not satisfy the range conditions of an actual image. This is precisely the issue behind sliced and Radon barycenter reconstructions discussed in Section OT Barycenters and illustrated in Figure Div.

Proposition: Metric Properties of Sliced Wasserstein

For p≥1p\geq1p≥1, SW⁡p\operatorname{SW}_pSWp​ is a distance on Pp(Rd)\mathcal P_p(\RR^d)Pp​(Rd). Moreover, SW⁡p\operatorname{SW}_pSWp​ metrizes weak convergence together with convergence of the pppth moment. Finally,

SW⁡p(α,β)≤Wp(α,β),\operatorname{SW}_p(\alpha,\beta)\leq\Wass_p(\alpha,\beta),SWp​(α,β)≤Wp​(α,β),
(46)

and, for p=2p=2p=2 with the uniform probability measure on the sphere,

SW⁡2(α,β)2≤1dW2(α,β)2.\operatorname{SW}_2(\alpha,\beta)^2 \leq \frac{1}{d}\Wass_2(\alpha,\beta)^2.SW2​(α,β)2≤d1​W2​(α,β)2.
(47)

Moreover, the sharp dimension-dependent comparison for p=1p=1p=1 has the form

W1(α,β)≤cdRd−1dSW⁡1(α,β)1d.\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta) \leq c_d R^{\frac{d-1}{d}}\operatorname{SW}_1(\alpha,\beta)^{\frac1d}.W1​(α,β)≤cd​Rdd−1​SW1​(α,β)d1​.

Proof

Non-negativity and symmetry follow from the one-dimensional Wasserstein distance. For the triangle inequality, apply the triangle inequality of Wp\Wass_pWp​ for each direction θ\thetaθ and then Minkowski’s inequality in Lp(Sd−1)L^p(\mathbb S^{d-1})Lp(Sd−1).

If SW⁡p(α,β)=0\operatorname{SW}_p(\alpha,\beta)=0SWp​(α,β)=0, then (Pθ)♯α=(Pθ)♯β(P_\theta)_\sharp\alpha=(P_\theta)_\sharp\beta(Pθ​)♯​α=(Pθ​)♯​β for almost every direction. By continuity of characteristic functions this holds for all directions, and the Cramer--Wold theorem implies α=β\alpha=\betaα=β.

The bound SW⁡p≤Wp\operatorname{SW}_p\leq\Wass_pSWp​≤Wp​ follows because PθP_\thetaPθ​ is 1-Lipschitz. For p=2p=2p=2, using any coupling π\piπ between α\alphaα and β\betaβ,

∫Sd−1∫∣⟨x−y,θ⟩∣2 dπ(x,y) dσ(θ)=1d∫∥x−y∥2 dπ(x,y).\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\int |\dotp{x-y}{\theta}|^2\d\pi(x,y)\d\sigma(\theta) = \frac{1}{d}\int \norm{x-y}^2\d\pi(x,y).∫Sd−1​∫∣⟨x−y,θ⟩∣2dπ(x,y)dσ(θ)=d1​∫∥x−y∥2dπ(x,y).

Optimizing over π\piπ gives the sharper inequality.

For the topology, Wp\Wass_pWp​ convergence implies sliced convergence by the upper bound. Conversely, if SW⁡p(αn,α)→0\operatorname{SW}_p(\alpha_n,\alpha)\to0SWp​(αn​,α)→0, then

∫Sd−1∫∣⟨θ,x⟩∣p dαn(x) dσ(θ)=cd,p∫∥x∥p dαn(x),cd,p>0,\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\int |\langle\theta,x\rangle|^p \d\alpha_n(x)\d\sigma(\theta) = c_{d,p}\int\|x\|^p\d\alpha_n(x), \qquad c_{d,p}>0,∫Sd−1​∫∣⟨θ,x⟩∣pdαn​(x)dσ(θ)=cd,p​∫∥x∥pdαn​(x),cd,p​>0,

and the projected-quantile formula give uniform moment bounds and hence tightness. Every subsequence has a further subsequence whose projected Wp\Wass_pWp​ distances vanish for almost every direction. Cramer--Wold identifies every weak limit with α\alphaα. If Qn,θQ_{n,\theta}Qn,θ​ and QθQ_\thetaQθ​ are the projected quantiles, then

SW⁡p(αn,α)=∥Qn,θ−Qθ∥Lp(Sd−1×(0,1)).\operatorname{SW}_p(\alpha_n,\alpha) = \|Q_{n,\theta}-Q_\theta\|_{L^p(\mathbb S^{d-1}\times(0,1))}.SWp​(αn​,α)=∥Qn,θ​−Qθ​∥Lp(Sd−1×(0,1))​.

Convergence of these LpL^pLp norms and the spherical identity yield convergence of the pppth moments. This is equivalent to Wp\Wass_pWp​ convergence.

The reverse estimates on compact sets are deeper and use the Radon structure of slices. Bonnotte’s Lemma 5.1.4 gives the historical exponent 1/(d+1)1/(d+1)1/(d+1) by mollifying a Kantorovich--Rubinstein test function, representing the regularized test through one-dimensional projections, bounding the resulting action by SW⁡1\operatorname{SW}_1SW1​, and optimizing the smoothing scale Bonnotte, 2013. The scaling in RRR follows by applying the unit-ball estimate to (x↦x/R)♯α(x\mapsto x/R)_\sharp\alpha(x↦x/R)♯​α and (x↦x/R)♯β(x\mapsto x/R)_\sharp\beta(x↦x/R)♯​β. The exponent 1/d1/d1/d is the sharp comparison theorem of Carlier, Figalli, Mérigot and Wang Carlier et al., 2025; their examples show that it cannot be improved in general.

The infinitesimal comparison is most transparent along smooth Brenier perturbations. A small gradient displacement is already optimal for the quadratic cost, and slicing simply tests its one-dimensional projections.

Proposition: First-Order Comparison Along Brenier Perturbations

Moreover,

SW⁡2(α,αt)2≤t2d∫Rd∥∇φ(x)∥2 dα(x).\SW_2(\alpha,\alpha_t)^2 \leq \frac{t^2}{d}\int_{\RR^d}\norm{\nabla\varphi(x)}^2\d\alpha(x).SW2​(α,αt​)2≤dt2​∫Rd​∥∇φ(x)∥2dα(x).

Remark: Sliced length and geodesic completion

There are two different geometries associated with SW⁡2\SW_2SW2​. The first is the chordal metric of Definition Definition: Sliced Wasserstein Distance, obtained by comparing all one-dimensional projections. The second is the intrinsic length metric generated by this chordal metric. If (αt)t∈[0,1](\alpha_t)_{t\in[0,1]}(αt​)t∈[0,1]​ is a continuous curve in (P2(Rd),SW⁡2)(\Pp_2(\RR^d),\SW_2)(P2​(Rd),SW2​), define

LSW⁡2((αt)t∈[0,1]):=sup⁡0=t0<⋯<tN=1∑i=0N−1SW⁡2(αti,αti+1),\mathsf L_{\SW_2}((\alpha_t)_{t\in[0,1]}) \eqdef \sup_{0=t_0<\cdots<t_N=1} \sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\SW_2(\alpha_{t_i},\alpha_{t_{i+1}}),LSW2​​((αt​)t∈[0,1]​):=0=t0​<⋯<tN​=1sup​i=0∑N−1​SW2​(αti​​,αti+1​​),
(58)

and

SW⁡2len(α,β):=inf⁡α0=α, α1=βt↦αt continuousLSW⁡2((αt)t∈[0,1]).\SW_2^{\mathrm{len}}(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \inf_{\substack{\alpha_0=\alpha,\ \alpha_1=\beta\\ t\mapsto\alpha_t\ \text{continuous}}} \mathsf L_{\SW_2}((\alpha_t)_{t\in[0,1]}).SW2len​(α,β):=α0​=α, α1​=βt↦αt​ continuous​inf​LSW2​​((αt​)t∈[0,1]​).
(59)

This length distance is always larger than the chordal distance SW⁡2\SW_2SW2​, but it should not be confused with the usual Wasserstein distance W2\Wass_2W2​. Recent work of Park and Slep\v{c}ev gives a systematic study of this sliced length geometry and shows in particular that the sliced Wasserstein space is not generally a length space Park & Slepčev, 2025.

Proposition Proposition: First-Order Comparison Along Brenier Perturbations is only an upper comparison of infinitesimal speeds. Along the same perturbation αt=(Id+t∇φ)♯α\alpha_t=(\Id+t\nabla\varphi)_\sharp\alphaαt​=(Id+t∇φ)♯​α, the W2\Wass_2W2​ metric derivative is the full norm ∥∇φ∥L2(α)\|\nabla\varphi\|_{L^2(\alpha)}∥∇φ∥L2(α)​. By contrast, the sliced metric derivative is obtained by projecting and then minimizing on each one-dimensional slice. Under standard smoothness assumptions, writing αθ=(Pθ)♯α\alpha_\theta=(P_\theta)_\sharp\alphaαθ​=(Pθ​)♯​α, the tangent formula of Park and Slepčev Park & Slepčev, 2025 gives

lim⁡t→0SW⁡2(α,αt)2t2=∫Sd−1∫R∣E[⟨θ,∇φ(X)⟩ | ⟨θ,X⟩=s]∣2 dαθ(s) dσ(θ),X∼α.\lim_{t\to0}\frac{\SW_2(\alpha,\alpha_t)^2}{t^2} = \int_{\Sphere^{d-1}}\int_\RR \abs{ \EE\left[\dotp{\theta}{\nabla\varphi(X)} \,\middle|\,\dotp{\theta}{X}=s\right]}^2 \d\alpha_\theta(s)\d\sigma(\theta), \qquad X\sim\alpha .t→0lim​t2SW2​(α,αt​)2​=∫Sd−1​∫R​∣E[⟨θ,∇φ(X)⟩∣⟨θ,X⟩=s]∣2dαθ​(s)dσ(θ),X∼α.
(60)

Jensen’s inequality gives the upper bound of Proposition Proposition: First-Order Comparison Along Brenier Perturbations, and the inequality is generally strict. Thus slicing preserves enough projected information to metrize the same topology as W2\Wass_2W2​, but it does not preserve the same Riemannian norm.

Proposition: Translations separate sliced length from W2\Wass_2W2​

Let τh(x)=x+h\tau_h(x)=x+hτh​(x)=x+h. For any α∈P2(Rd)\alpha\in\Pp_2(\RR^d)α∈P2​(Rd),

SW⁡2len(α,(τh)♯α)=SW⁡2(α,(τh)♯α)=∥h∥d,W2(α,(τh)♯α)=∥h∥.\SW_2^{\mathrm{len}}\big(\alpha,(\tau_h)_\sharp\alpha\big) = \SW_2\big(\alpha,(\tau_h)_\sharp\alpha\big) = \frac{\norm{h}}{\sqrt d}, \qquad \Wass_2\big(\alpha,(\tau_h)_\sharp\alpha\big)=\norm{h}.SW2len​(α,(τh​)♯​α)=SW2​(α,(τh​)♯​α)=d​∥h∥​,W2​(α,(τh​)♯​α)=∥h∥.

Proof

For each direction θ\thetaθ, the projected measure (Pθ)♯(τh)♯α(P_\theta)_\sharp(\tau_h)_\sharp\alpha(Pθ​)♯​(τh​)♯​α is the translate of (Pθ)♯α(P_\theta)_\sharp\alpha(Pθ​)♯​α by the scalar ⟨θ,h⟩\dotp{\theta}{h}⟨θ,h⟩. Hence the one-dimensional squared distance is ∣⟨θ,h⟩∣2\abs{\dotp{\theta}{h}}^2∣⟨θ,h⟩∣2, and integrating over directions gives SW⁡22=∥h∥2/d\SW_2^2=\norm{h}^2/dSW22​=∥h∥2/d.

The proposition is the useful sanity check: the geodesic completion suggested by slicing is a projected sliced geometry, not the usual displacement geometry. Straight chords in the projected-quantile Hilbert embedding below need not satisfy the consistency constraints required to come from actual measures on Rd\RR^dRd.

Remark: Hilbert embedding for SW⁡2\SW_2SW2​

In one dimension, W2\Wass_2W2​ is the L2(0,1)L^2(0,1)L2(0,1) distance between quantile functions. Hence

SW⁡2(α,β)2=∫Sd−1∫01∣Fθ,α−1(u)−Fθ,β−1(u)∣2 du dσ(θ),\SW_2(\alpha,\beta)^2 = \int_{\Sphere^{d-1}}\int_0^1 \abs{F_{\theta,\alpha}^{-1}(u)-F_{\theta,\beta}^{-1}(u)}^2 \d u\d\sigma(\theta),SW2​(α,β)2=∫Sd−1​∫01​∣∣​Fθ,α−1​(u)−Fθ,β−1​(u)∣∣​2dudσ(θ),
(62)

where Fθ,α−1F_{\theta,\alpha}^{-1}Fθ,α−1​ is the quantile of (Pθ)♯α(P_\theta)_\sharp\alpha(Pθ​)♯​α. Thus SW⁡2\SW_2SW2​ is a Hilbertian distance after embedding each measure into its field of projected quantiles. Consequently, exp⁡(−γSW⁡22)\exp(-\gamma\SW_2^2)exp(−γSW22​) is a positive definite kernel on probability measures for every γ>0\gamma>0γ>0.

The compact reverse estimates in Proposition Proposition: Metric Properties of Sliced Wasserstein explain why sliced distances metrize the same topology on bounded sets, while the dimension-dependent powers prevent a dimension-free bi-Lipschitz comparison with Wp\Wass_pWp​.

Definition: Max-Sliced Wasserstein

The max-sliced distance replaces the average over directions by the most discriminating one:

MaxSW⁡p(α,β):=sup⁡θ∈Sd−1Wp((Pθ)♯α,(Pθ)♯β).\operatorname{MaxSW}_p(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \sup_{\theta\in\mathbb S^{d-1}} \Wass_p((P_\theta)_\sharp\alpha,(P_\theta)_\sharp\beta).MaxSWp​(α,β):=θ∈Sd−1sup​Wp​((Pθ​)♯​α,(Pθ​)♯​β).
(63)

Subspace-Sliced Variants¶

One-dimensional slices are extremely cheap, but they may discard too much geometry in high dimension. A natural compromise is to project onto kkk-dimensional subspaces: the projected OT problems remain lower dimensional, while each projection retains correlations inside a small block of coordinates.

Definition: Subspace-Sliced Wasserstein

Fix 1≤k≤d1\leq k\leq d1≤k≤d. Subspace-sliced variants replace one-dimensional lines by kkk-dimensional orthogonal projections. If U∈Rd×kU\in\RR^{d\times k}U∈Rd×k satisfies U⊤U=IkU^\top U=I_kU⊤U=Ik​, then

SW⁡p,k(α,β)p:=∫Wp((U⊤)♯α,(U⊤)♯β)p dU,\operatorname{SW}_{p,k}(\alpha,\beta)^p \eqdef \int \Wass_p((U^\top)_\sharp\alpha,(U^\top)_\sharp\beta)^p\d U,SWp,k​(α,β)p:=∫Wp​((U⊤)♯​α,(U⊤)♯​β)pdU,
(64)

where  dU\d UdU denotes the normalized invariant measure on the Stiefel manifold St⁡(d,k)={U∈Rd×k:U⊤U=Ik}\operatorname{St}(d,k)=\{U\in\RR^{d\times k}:U^\top U=I_k\}St(d,k)={U∈Rd×k:U⊤U=Ik​}, and

MaxSW⁡p,k(α,β):=sup⁡U⊤U=IkWp((U⊤)♯α,(U⊤)♯β).\operatorname{MaxSW}_{p,k}(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \sup_{U^\top U=I_k} \Wass_p((U^\top)_\sharp\alpha,(U^\top)_\sharp\beta).MaxSWp,k​(α,β):=U⊤U=Ik​sup​Wp​((U⊤)♯​α,(U⊤)♯​β).
(65)

The case k=1k=1k=1 recovers ordinary sliced and max-sliced Wasserstein, while k=dk=dk=d recovers the original Wasserstein distance.

Proposition: Basic Bounds for Sliced Variants

Let p≥1p\geq1p≥1 and let α,β∈Pp(Rd)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal P_p(\RR^d)α,β∈Pp​(Rd). With normalized spherical and Stiefel measures,

SW⁡p(α,β)≤MaxSW⁡p(α,β)≤Wp(α,β).\operatorname{SW}_p(\alpha,\beta) \leq \operatorname{MaxSW}_p(\alpha,\beta) \leq \Wass_p(\alpha,\beta).SWp​(α,β)≤MaxSWp​(α,β)≤Wp​(α,β).
(66)

For kkk-dimensional subspace projections,

SW⁡p,k(α,β)≤MaxSW⁡p,k(α,β)≤Wp(α,β).\operatorname{SW}_{p,k}(\alpha,\beta) \leq \operatorname{MaxSW}_{p,k}(\alpha,\beta) \leq \Wass_p(\alpha,\beta).SWp,k​(α,β)≤MaxSWp,k​(α,β)≤Wp​(α,β).
(67)

For p=2p=2p=2, rotational invariance gives the sharper estimate

SW⁡2,k(α,β)2≤kdW2(α,β)2.\operatorname{SW}_{2,k}(\alpha,\beta)^2 \leq \frac{k}{d}\Wass_2(\alpha,\beta)^2.SW2,k​(α,β)2≤dk​W2​(α,β)2.
(68)
Proof

The first inequality in each line follows because an LpL^pLp average over a probability space is bounded by the corresponding supremum. The second inequality follows because orthogonal projections are 1-Lipschitz: pushing any admissible coupling between α\alphaα and β\betaβ through a projection gives an admissible coupling for the projected measures with no larger transport cost. Optimizing over couplings and then averaging or maximizing over the projection gives the result.

For the last estimate, use ∫St⁡(d,k)∥U⊤z∥2 dU=(k/d)∥z∥2\int_{\operatorname{St}(d,k)}\|U^\top z\|^2\d U=(k/d)\|z\|^2∫St(d,k)​∥U⊤z∥2dU=(k/d)∥z∥2 under any coupling, and then minimize over couplings.

Min-Sliced Lifted Transport Plans¶

The preceding constructions define distances between projected measures. A different use of slicing is to use a projection only as a device for building a feasible high-dimensional transport plan. For equal-weight empirical measures α=n−1∑iδxi\alpha=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{x_i}α=n−1∑i​δxi​​ and β=n−1∑iδyi\beta=n^{-1}\sum_i\delta_{y_i}β=n−1∑i​δyi​​, sort the projected samples ⟨xi,θ⟩\dotp{x_i}{\theta}⟨xi​,θ⟩ and ⟨yj,θ⟩\dotp{y_j}{\theta}⟨yj​,θ⟩, and let σθ\sigma_\thetaσθ​ be the monotone matching induced by this sorting. The lifted plan

πθ=1n∑i=1nδ(xi,yσθ(i))\pi_\theta = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \delta_{(x_i,y_{\sigma_\theta(i)})}πθ​=n1​i=1∑n​δ(xi​,yσθ​(i)​)​
(69)

is a genuine coupling between α\alphaα and β\betaβ in the original space. Min-SWGG-type methods then choose the projection whose lifted plan has the smallest full-dimensional quadratic cost:

MSWGG⁡2(α,β)2:=min⁡θ∈Sd−1∫∥x−y∥2 dπθ(x,y).\operatorname{MSWGG}_2(\alpha,\beta)^2 \eqdef \min_{\theta\in\mathbb S^{d-1}} \int\norm{x-y}^2\d\pi_\theta(x,y).MSWGG2​(α,β)2:=θ∈Sd−1min​∫∥x−y∥2dπθ​(x,y).
(70)

This is the min-SWGG construction of Mahey, Chapel, Gasso, Bonet and Courty Mahey et al., 2023. It is not a projected distance but a cheap feasible-plan construction. Consequently,

W22(α,β)≤∫∥x−y∥2 dπθ(x,y),W22(α,β)≤MSWGG⁡2(α,β)2.\Wass_2^2(\alpha,\beta) \leq \int\norm{x-y}^2\d\pi_\theta(x,y), \qquad \Wass_2^2(\alpha,\beta) \leq \operatorname{MSWGG}_2(\alpha,\beta)^2.W22​(α,β)≤∫∥x−y∥2dπθ​(x,y),W22​(α,β)≤MSWGG2​(α,β)2.
(71)

Quotient Wasserstein and Wasserstein-Procrustes¶

Many comparison problems contain nuisance transformations: two shapes, images or point clouds should be considered close after translating, rotating or otherwise reparametrizing one of them. Quotient Wasserstein distances encode this idea by computing transport after optimizing over a group action. This construction is the metric analogue of passing from objects to shapes modulo symmetries, and connects OT with shape spaces, metamorphosis models and global-invariance variants of transport Trouvé & Younes, 2005Zemel & Panaretos, 2019Alvarez-Melis et al., 2019.

Definition: Quotient Wasserstein Distance

Let a group G\mathcal GG act on a metric space (X,d)(\Xx,d)(X,d) by isometries, and assume that the action preserves finite pppth moments. Write g♯αg_\sharp\alphag♯​α for the push-forward of a measure α\alphaα by g∈Gg\in\mathcal Gg∈G, and write [α]:={g♯α:g∈G}[\alpha]\eqdef\{g_\sharp\alpha:g\in\mathcal G\}[α]:={g♯​α:g∈G} for its orbit. The quotient ppp-Wasserstein distance between the orbits of α,β∈Pp(X)\alpha,\beta\in\Pp_p(\Xx)α,β∈Pp​(X) is

Wp,G([α],[β]):=inf⁡g,h∈GWp(g♯α,h♯β)=inf⁡g∈GWp(α,g♯β).\Wass_{p,\mathcal G}([\alpha],[\beta]) \eqdef \inf_{g,h\in\mathcal G}\Wass_p(g_\sharp\alpha,h_\sharp\beta) = \inf_{g\in\mathcal G}\Wass_p(\alpha,g_\sharp\beta).Wp,G​([α],[β]):=g,h∈Ginf​Wp​(g♯​α,h♯​β)=g∈Ginf​Wp​(α,g♯​β).
(72)
Proposition: Metric Property on the Quotient

If G\mathcal GG acts by isometries and preserves Pp(X)\Pp_p(\Xx)Pp​(X), then Wp,G\Wass_{p,\mathcal G}Wp,G​ is a pseudo-distance on Pp(X)\Pp_p(\Xx)Pp​(X). If, in addition, the infimum is attained between every pair of orbits, then it is a distance on the orbit space Pp(X)/G\Pp_p(\Xx)/\mathcal GPp​(X)/G. This applies in particular to continuous actions of compact groups.

Proof

Isometry of the action gives Wp(g♯α,g♯β)=Wp(α,β)\Wass_p(g_\sharp\alpha,g_\sharp\beta)=\Wass_p(\alpha,\beta)Wp​(g♯​α,g♯​β)=Wp​(α,β), which proves the second formula above. Non-negativity and symmetry are inherited from Wp\Wass_pWp​. For the triangle inequality, choose g1,g2∈Gg_1,g_2\in\mathcal Gg1​,g2​∈G and write

Wp(α,(g1)♯β)+Wp(β,(g2)♯γ)=Wp(α,(g1)♯β)+Wp((g1)♯β,(g1g2)♯γ).\Wass_p(\alpha,(g_1)_\sharp\beta) + \Wass_p(\beta,(g_2)_\sharp\gamma) = \Wass_p(\alpha,(g_1)_\sharp\beta) + \Wass_p((g_1)_\sharp\beta,(g_1g_2)_\sharp\gamma).Wp​(α,(g1​)♯​β)+Wp​(β,(g2​)♯​γ)=Wp​(α,(g1​)♯​β)+Wp​((g1​)♯​β,(g1​g2​)♯​γ).
(73)

The triangle inequality for Wp\Wass_pWp​, followed by the infimum over g1,g2g_1,g_2g1​,g2​, gives the result. If the infimum is attained and the quotient distance is zero, there exist g,h∈Gg,h\in\mathcal Gg,h∈G such that Wp(g♯α,h♯β)=0\Wass_p(g_\sharp\alpha,h_\sharp\beta)=0Wp​(g♯​α,h♯​β)=0, hence g♯α=h♯βg_\sharp\alpha=h_\sharp\betag♯​α=h♯​β, which is exactly equality of the two orbits. For compact groups, continuity of the action and compactness give the required attainment. Without attainment, distinct orbits at zero orbit distance must be identified to obtain a genuine metric space.

Rigid Motions and Wasserstein-Procrustes¶

The most common example is the Euclidean group E(d)=O(d)⋉Rd\mathrm E(d)=\mathrm O(d)\ltimes\RR^dE(d)=O(d)⋉Rd. For measures on Rd\RR^dRd, quotienting by rotations and translations gives the Wasserstein-Procrustes problem

inf⁡R∈O(d), t∈Rd, π∈Π(α,β)∫∥Rx+t−y∥2 dπ(x,y).\inf_{R\in\mathrm O(d),\,t\in\RR^d,\,\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int\norm{Rx+t-y}^2\d\pi(x,y).R∈O(d),t∈Rd,π∈Π(α,β)inf​∫∥Rx+t−y∥2dπ(x,y).
(74)

Replacing O(d)\mathrm O(d)O(d) by SO(d)\mathrm{SO}(d)SO(d) enforces orientation preservation. This is the case p=2p=2p=2 of the quotient distance; for a general exponent ppp, one replaces the quadratic cost by the pppth power of the Euclidean distance. Although the translation group is noncompact, the quadratic problem is well behaved: for fixed RRR and π\piπ, the optimal translation aligns RxˉR\bar xRxˉ with yˉ\bar yyˉ​. The remaining rigid step is therefore an orthogonal Procrustes problem over the compact group O(d)\mathrm O(d)O(d).

For empirical measures, this couples a transport problem with a rigid registration problem. Classical iterative closest point methods alternate nearest-neighbor assignment and rigid least squares Besl & McKay, 1992. Wasserstein-Procrustes replaces these hard many-to-one nearest-neighbor correspondences by a mass-preserving OT plan. This makes the registration less tied to sampling density and better suited to ambiguous correspondences.

Two complementary machine-learning formulations clarify the scope of this construction. Grave, Joulin and Berthet Grave et al., 2019 formulate unsupervised alignment of high-dimensional embeddings as a Wasserstein-Procrustes problem. In their equal-weight setting, one jointly estimates an orthogonal matrix and a permutation; they use a convex-relaxation initialization and a stochastic large-scale solver, with bilingual lexicon induction as the main application. Alvarez-Melis, Jegelka and Jaakkola Alvarez-Melis et al., 2019 place the same idea in a broader framework: the coupling and a latent global transformation are optimized jointly over a flexible invariance class because cross-space costs are otherwise ill-defined. The rigid quadratic model and block updates below are the isometric Procrustes specialization of this global-invariance viewpoint.

This is an extrinsic counterpart of the Gromov--Wasserstein viewpoint developed in Gromov--Wasserstein. Procrustes alignment searches only over ambient rigid motions, whereas GW is invariant under intrinsic measure-preserving isometries. If both spaces are Euclidean and Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣\Delta(u,v)=|u-v|Δ(u,v)=∣u−v∣, then rigid motions preserve all within-space distances and do not change the metric-measure isometry class. Applying the Euclidean GW/Wasserstein estimate to the aligned pair, and then taking the infimum over rigid motions, gives

GW⁡((Rd,∥⋅∥,α),(Rd,∥⋅∥,β))≤2 Wp,E(d)([α],[β]).\operatorname{GW}((\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\alpha),(\RR^d,\norm{\cdot},\beta)) \leq 2\,\Wass_{p,\mathrm E(d)}([\alpha],[\beta]).GW((Rd,∥⋅∥,α),(Rd,∥⋅∥,β))≤2Wp,E(d)​([α],[β]).
(75)

Thus a good Wasserstein-Procrustes registration certifies small GW distortion. The converse need not hold: GW may be small because of an intrinsic correspondence that is not induced by an ambient rigid motion. The Mémoli profile lower bound in Proposition: Memoli Profile Lower Bound gives the complementary intrinsic lower certificate.

The empirical problem naturally suggests an alternating minimization. Given a current rigid motion (R(k),t(k))(R^{(k)},t^{(k)})(R(k),t(k)), first compute the OT coupling between the registered source cloud and the target cloud,

P(k)∈arg min⁡P∈U(a,b)∑i,jPij∥R(k)xi+t(k)−yj∥2.\P^{(k)} \in \argmin_{\P\in\CouplingsD(\a,\b)} \sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}\norm{R^{(k)}x_i+t^{(k)}-y_j}^2 .P(k)∈P∈U(a,b)argmin​i,j∑​Pij​∥∥​R(k)xi​+t(k)−yj​∥∥​2.
(76)

Then freeze this coupling and update the rigid motion by

(R(k+1),t(k+1))∈arg min⁡R∈O(d), t∈Rd∑i,jPij(k)∥Rxi+t−yj∥2,(R^{(k+1)},t^{(k+1)}) \in \argmin_{R\in\mathrm O(d),\,t\in\RR^d} \sum_{i,j}\P^{(k)}_{ij}\norm{Rx_i+t-y_j}^2 ,(R(k+1),t(k+1))∈R∈O(d),t∈Rdargmin​i,j∑​Pij(k)​∥Rxi​+t−yj​∥2,
(77)

or by the same formula with R∈SO(d)R\in\mathrm{SO}(d)R∈SO(d) if orientation should be preserved. The first step is an ordinary discrete OT problem with the current registered cost matrix; the next proposition shows that the second step is an orthogonal Procrustes problem with an explicit singular-value formula.

Proposition: Rigid Update for a Fixed Coupling

Let α=∑iaiδxi\alpha=\sum_i a_i\delta_{x_i}α=∑i​ai​δxi​​ and β=∑jbjδyj\beta=\sum_j b_j\delta_{y_j}β=∑j​bj​δyj​​, and fix P∈U(a,b)\P\in\CouplingsD(\a,\b)P∈U(a,b). Define

xˉ=∑iaixi,yˉ=∑jbjyj,MP=∑i,jPij(yj−yˉ)(xi−xˉ)⊤.\bar x=\sum_i a_i x_i,\qquad \bar y=\sum_j b_j y_j,\qquad M_\P=\sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}(y_j-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)^\top .xˉ=i∑​ai​xi​,yˉ​=j∑​bj​yj​,MP​=i,j∑​Pij​(yj​−yˉ​)(xi​−xˉ)⊤.
(78)

If MP=UΣV⊤M_\P=U\Sigma V^\topMP​=UΣV⊤ is a singular value decomposition, then the minimizers over the full orthogonal group of

min⁡R∈O(d), t∈Rd∑i,jPij∥Rxi+t−yj∥2\min_{R\in\mathrm O(d),\,t\in\RR^d} \sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}\norm{Rx_i+t-y_j}^2R∈O(d),t∈Rdmin​i,j∑​Pij​∥Rxi​+t−yj​∥2
(79)

are given by R⋆=UV⊤R^\star=UV^\topR⋆=UV⊤ and t⋆=yˉ−R⋆xˉt^\star=\bar y-R^\star\bar xt⋆=yˉ​−R⋆xˉ, up to the usual non-uniqueness when MPM_\PMP​ is rank deficient. If one imposes R∈SO(d)R\in\mathrm{SO}(d)R∈SO(d), set

D=diag⁡(1,…,1,det⁡(UV⊤)),R⋆=UDV⊤,t⋆=yˉ−R⋆xˉ.D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\ldots,1,\det(UV^\top)), \qquad R^\star=UDV^\top, \qquad t^\star=\bar y-R^\star\bar x .D=diag(1,…,1,det(UV⊤)),R⋆=UDV⊤,t⋆=yˉ​−R⋆xˉ.
(80)
Proof

For fixed RRR, differentiating with respect to ttt gives t=yˉ−Rxˉt=\bar y-R\bar xt=yˉ​−Rxˉ. Substituting this value centers the variables and leaves

∑i,jPij∥R(xi−xˉ)−(yj−yˉ)∥2.\sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}\norm{R(x_i-\bar x)-(y_j-\bar y)}^2.i,j∑​Pij​∥R(xi​−xˉ)−(yj​−yˉ​)∥2.
(81)

The two quadratic terms independent of RRR are fixed, so the problem is equivalent to maximizing ∑i,jPij⟨R(xi−xˉ),yj−yˉ⟩=tr⁡(R⊤MP)\sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}\dotp{R(x_i-\bar x)}{y_j-\bar y} =\tr(R^\top M_\P)∑i,j​Pij​⟨R(xi​−xˉ),yj​−yˉ​⟩=tr(R⊤MP​). Von Neumann’s trace inequality gives the maximum for R=UV⊤R=UV^\topR=UV⊤. Under the constraint R∈SO(d)R\in\mathrm{SO}(d)R∈SO(d), the same argument applies with the additional determinant constraint on U⊤RVU^\top R VU⊤RV, which gives the displayed diagonal correction.

Equations (76)--(77) give a block-coordinate method. The objective is not jointly convex, so the scheme should be read as a registration heuristic for the quotient problem rather than as a global solver. The exact block update moves the rigid motion fully; for visualization or continuation, one may damp the displayed motion between two successive poses.

Algorithm: Alternating Wasserstein--Procrustes alignment

Input: Weighted point clouds (xi,ai)i=1n(x_i,\a_i)_{i=1}^n(xi​,ai​)i=1n​, (yj,bj)j=1m(y_j,\b_j)_{j=1}^m(yj​,bj​)j=1m​, initial rigid motion (R(0),t(0))(R^{(0)},t^{(0)})(R(0),t(0)), tolerance tol\mathrm{tol}tol, choice O(d)\mathrm O(d)O(d) or SO(d)\mathrm{SO}(d)SO(d).

Output: Last coupling P\PP and rigid motion (R,t)(R,t)(R,t).

Set xˉ=∑iaixi\bar x=\sum_i\a_i x_ixˉ=∑i​ai​xi​, yˉ=∑jbjyj\bar y=\sum_j\b_j y_jyˉ​=∑j​bj​yj​, k=0k=0k=0 and η0=+∞\eta_0=+\inftyη0​=+∞.

While ηk>tol\eta_k>\mathrm{tol}ηk​>tol do:

Set Cij(k)=∥R(k)xi+t(k)−yj∥2C_{ij}^{(k)}=\norm{R^{(k)}x_i+t^{(k)}-y_j}^2Cij(k)​=∥∥​R(k)xi​+t(k)−yj​∥∥​2.

Solve P(k)∈arg min⁡P∈U(a,b)∑i,jPijCij(k)\P^{(k)}\in\argmin_{\P\in\CouplingsD(\a,\b)}\sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}C_{ij}^{(k)}P(k)∈argminP∈U(a,b)​∑i,j​Pij​Cij(k)​.

Compute MP(k)=∑i,jPij(k)(yj−yˉ)(xi−xˉ)⊤M_{\P^{(k)}}=\sum_{i,j}\P^{(k)}_{ij}(y_j-\bar y)(x_i-\bar x)^\topMP(k)​=∑i,j​Pij(k)​(yj​−yˉ​)(xi​−xˉ)⊤.

Factorize MP(k)=UΣV⊤M_{\P^{(k)}}=U\Sigma V^\topMP(k)​=UΣV⊤.

Set D=IdD=\IdD=Id for O(d)\mathrm O(d)O(d); set D=diag⁡(1,…,1,det⁡(UV⊤))D=\diag(1,\ldots,1,\det(UV^\top))D=diag(1,…,1,det(UV⊤)) for SO(d)\mathrm{SO}(d)SO(d).

Set R(k+1)=UDV⊤R^{(k+1)}=UDV^\topR(k+1)=UDV⊤ and t(k+1)=yˉ−R(k+1)xˉt^{(k+1)}=\bar y-R^{(k+1)}\bar xt(k+1)=yˉ​−R(k+1)xˉ.

Set ηk+1=∥R(k+1)−R(k)∥F+∥t(k+1)−t(k)∥\eta_{k+1}=\norm{R^{(k+1)}-R^{(k)}}_{\mathrm F}+\norm{t^{(k+1)}-t^{(k)}}ηk+1​=∥∥​R(k+1)−R(k)∥∥​F​+∥∥​t(k+1)−t(k)∥∥​.

Set k←k+1k\leftarrow k+1k←k+1.

Solve P(k)∈arg min⁡P∈U(a,b)∑i,jPij∥R(k)xi+t(k)−yj∥2\P^{(k)}\in\argmin_{\P\in\CouplingsD(\a,\b)} \sum_{i,j}\P_{ij}\norm{R^{(k)}x_i+t^{(k)}-y_j}^2P(k)∈argminP∈U(a,b)​∑i,j​Pij​∥∥​R(k)xi​+t(k)−yj​∥∥​2.

Return P(k),R(k),t(k)\P^{(k)},R^{(k)},t^{(k)}P(k),R(k),t(k).

Vector Quantiles and Linear Optimal Transport¶

Linear OT starts from the multivariate analogue of quantile coordinates. The one-dimensional quantile function represents a probability measure by the monotone map sending a fixed reference law to it; in dimension d>1d>1d>1, Brenier’s theorem gives the corresponding construction after choosing an absolutely continuous reference probability ρ\rhoρ, typically the uniform law on a convex body or a standard Gaussian.

Vector Quantiles¶

Assume that ρ\rhoρ is absolutely continuous. For a target law α\alα with finite second moment, its vector quantile relative to ρ\rhoρ is the Brenier map

Tα=∇ϕα,(Tα)♯ρ=α,T_\al=\nabla\phi_\al, \qquad (T_\al)_\sharp\rho=\al,Tα​=∇ϕα​,(Tα​)♯​ρ=α,
(82)

or equivalently the solution of

min⁡T♯ρ=α∫∥x−T(x)∥2 dρ(x).\min_{T_\sharp\rho=\al} \int\norm{x-T(x)}^2\d\rho(x).T♯​ρ=αmin​∫∥x−T(x)∥2dρ(x).
(83)

This construction is canonical only after fixing ρ\rhoρ: changing the reference law changes the coordinates used to represent α\alα. Vector quantile regression uses the same idea conditionally, replacing scalar conditional quantiles by conditional Brenier maps and thereby encoding multivariate ranks and depths Carlier et al., 2017.

Linearized Wasserstein Coordinates¶

Linear OT replaces a nonlinear transport distance by a Hilbert norm between reference maps. It is useful when one reference measure is fixed and many nearby distributions must be compared cheaply. Let TαT_\alphaTα​ be the Brenier map pushing ρ\rhoρ to α\alphaα, understood as an element of L2(ρ;Rd)L^2(\rho;\RR^d)L2(ρ;Rd) and hence defined only ρ\rhoρ-almost everywhere. The linear OT embedding is

α↦Tα−Id∈L2(ρ;Rd),LOT⁡ρ(α,β)=∥Tα−Tβ∥L2(ρ).\alpha\mapsto T_\alpha-\Id\in L^2(\rho;\RR^d), \qquad \operatorname{LOT}_\rho(\alpha,\beta) = \norm{T_\alpha-T_\beta}_{L^2(\rho)}.α↦Tα​−Id∈L2(ρ;Rd),LOTρ​(α,β)=∥Tα​−Tβ​∥L2(ρ)​.
(84)

If one of the two targets equals the reference, the linearized distance is exact: for instance, LOT⁡ρ(ρ,α)=∥Tα−Id∥L2(ρ)=W2(ρ,α)\operatorname{LOT}_\rho(\rho,\alpha) =\norm{T_\alpha-\Id}_{L^2(\rho)} =\Wass_2(\rho,\alpha)LOTρ​(ρ,α)=∥Tα​−Id∥L2(ρ)​=W2​(ρ,α). For two arbitrary targets, the coupling (Tα,Tβ)♯ρ(T_\alpha,T_\beta)_\sharp\rho(Tα​,Tβ​)♯​ρ is admissible but not generally optimal, so LOT⁡ρ\operatorname{LOT}_\rhoLOTρ​ is a tangent-space approximation of the Wasserstein geometry Wang et al., 2013. Uniqueness of the Brenier maps also shows that LOT⁡ρ\operatorname{LOT}_\rhoLOTρ​ is a genuine distance on the class of targets for which these maps are defined.

For a family (αs)s(\alpha_s)_s(αs​)s​ with weights (λs)s(\lambda_s)_s(λs​)s​, the linearized barycenter is obtained by averaging maps,

Tˉ=∑sλsTαs,αˉLOT⁡=Tˉ♯ρ.\bar T=\sum_s\lambda_s T_{\alpha_s}, \qquad \bar\alpha_{\operatorname{LOT}}=\bar T_\sharp\rho.Tˉ=s∑​λs​Tαs​​,αˉLOT​=Tˉ♯​ρ.
(85)

This is exact in one dimension, where quantile functions linearize W2\Wass_2W2​, and it is especially useful when many barycenters with changing weights must be evaluated quickly.

Principal Components in Linear OT Coordinates¶

The preceding embedding turns probability measures into displacement fields in a fixed Hilbert chart, so ordinary principal component analysis can be applied to deformations rather than to densities. Given training measures (αi)i=1N(\alpha_i)_{i=1}^N(αi​)i=1N​, set

zi:=Tαi−Id,zˉ:=1N∑i=1Nzi.z_i \eqdef T_{\alpha_i}-\Id, \qquad \bar z \eqdef \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N z_i .zi​:=Tαi​​−Id,zˉ:=N1​i=1∑N​zi​.
(86)

The map Id+zˉ\Id+\bar zId+zˉ defines the linear OT mean (Id+zˉ)♯ρ(\Id+\bar z)_\sharp\rho(Id+zˉ)♯​ρ. The empirical covariance operator on L2(ρ;Rd)L^2(\rho;\RR^d)L2(ρ;Rd) is the finite-rank operator

CLOT⁡h:=1N∑i=1N⟨zi−zˉ,h⟩L2(ρ)(zi−zˉ),\mathcal C_{\operatorname{LOT}} h \eqdef \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \dotp{z_i-\bar z}{h}_{L^2(\rho)} (z_i-\bar z),CLOT​h:=N1​i=1∑N​⟨zi​−zˉ,h⟩L2(ρ)​(zi​−zˉ),
(87)

and its leading orthonormal eigenvectors eke_kek​ define the principal linear OT modes. Equivalently, one diagonalizes the N×NN\times NN×N Gram matrix Gij=1N⟨zi−zˉ,zj−zˉ⟩L2(ρ)G_{ij}=\frac1N\dotp{z_i-\bar z}{z_j-\bar z}_{L^2(\rho)}Gij​=N1​⟨zi​−zˉ,zj​−zˉ⟩L2(ρ)​. If Gv(k)=λkv(k)Gv^{(k)}=\lambda_k v^{(k)}Gv(k)=λk​v(k) with λk>0\lambda_k>0λk​>0 and ∥v(k)∥=1\norm{v^{(k)}}=1∥∥​v(k)∥∥​=1, then

ek=1Nλk∑i=1Nvi(k)(zi−zˉ)e_k=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N\lambda_k}}\sum_{i=1}^N v_i^{(k)}(z_i-\bar z)ek​=Nλk​​1​i=1∑N​vi(k)​(zi​−zˉ)
(88)

is the corresponding unit eigenvector of CLOT⁡\mathcal C_{\operatorname{LOT}}CLOT​. The score of αi\alpha_iαi​ along mode eke_kek​ is

ai,k:=⟨zi−zˉ,ek⟩L2(ρ).a_{i,k} \eqdef \dotp{z_i-\bar z}{e_k}_{L^2(\rho)} .ai,k​:=⟨zi​−zˉ,ek​⟩L2(ρ)​.
(89)

A low-rank reconstruction, or a synthetic excursion with prescribed coefficients a=(a1,…,am)a=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)a=(a1​,…,am​), is then obtained by pushing the reference through

Ta(x):=x+zˉ(x)+∑k=1makek(x),αa:=(Ta)♯ρ.T_a(x) \eqdef x+\bar z(x)+\sum_{k=1}^m a_k e_k(x), \qquad \alpha_a \eqdef (T_a)_\sharp\rho .Ta​(x):=x+zˉ(x)+k=1∑m​ak​ek​(x),αa​:=(Ta​)♯​ρ.
(90)

For small excursions around the mean displacement, this gives a practical tangent-space PCA for probability measures: it captures dominant modes of deformation while avoiding repeated pairwise OT computations. For large coefficients, TaT_aTa​ may fail to be the Brenier map from ρ\rhoρ to αa\alpha_aαa​, and may even leave the regular chart where TaT_aTa​ is a gradient of a convex function. Thus the curve a↦αaa\mapsto\alpha_aa↦αa​ should be read as a chart-dependent linearized visualization rather than as an intrinsic Wasserstein geodesic. This LOT-PCA viewpoint was introduced for image variability analysis in Wang et al., 2013 and developed in transport-based signal analysis Thorpe et al., 2017Kolouri et al., 2017; it complements intrinsic principal-geodesic or geodesic-PCA approaches, which optimize directly in the curved Wasserstein space Seguy & Cuturi, 2015Bigot et al., 2017.

Remark: Three Hilbertian embeddings of measures

Several constructions in this text embed measures into Hilbert spaces, but they encode different geometries. Kernel mean embeddings send α\alphaα to ∫k(x,⋅) dα(x)\int k(x,\cdot)\d\alpha(x)∫k(x,⋅)dα(x) in an RKHS and lead to MMD distances; see Section Dual RKHS Norms and Maximum Mean Discrepancies. Quadratic sliced Wasserstein sends a measure to the collection of one-dimensional quantile functions of its projections, viewed in L2(Sd−1×[0,1])L^2(\Sphere^{d-1}\times[0,1])L2(Sd−1×[0,1]); see Section Sliced Wasserstein Distances. Linear OT sends α\alphaα to the displacement field Tα−IdT_\alpha-\IdTα​−Id from a fixed reference ρ\rhoρ in L2(ρ;Rd)L^2(\rho;\RR^d)L2(ρ;Rd). The first construction is linear in the measure and depends on the kernel, the second is nonlinear but reduces OT to projected one-dimensional quantiles, and the third is a tangent approximation to the full Wasserstein geometry around a chosen reference.

show_book_figure("dualnorms-linear-ot-embedding")

Linear OT coordinates. Fixing a reference measure ρ\rhoρ turns each target into a map TαT_\alphaTα​ from ρ\rhoρ to α\alphaα, or equivalently into the displacement field Tα−IdT_\alpha-\IdTα​−Id. In one dimension this is exactly the quantile parametrization of W2\Wass_2W2​. In two dimensions, averaging the maps gives the linearized barycenter, which is compared with the genuine McCann midpoint.

The next control keeps the exact one-dimensional setting. The reference density defines the coordinate system, the target maps are quantile maps from that reference, and the barycenter is obtained by averaging those maps before pushing the reference forward.

Interactive panel. Use the reference and deformation controls to inspect how linear optimal transport embeds measures through maps from a fixed template.

Proposition: Quantitative Stability of Linear OT

Let X,Y⊂RdX,Y\subset\RR^dX,Y⊂Rd be compact convex sets, assume that XXX has positive Lebesgue measure, and let ρ\rhoρ be normalized Lebesgue measure on XXX. There is a constant C=C(d,X,Y)C=C(d,X,Y)C=C(d,X,Y) such that, for all α,β∈P(Y)\alpha,\beta\in\mathcal P(Y)α,β∈P(Y),

W2(α,β)≤LOT⁡ρ(α,β)andLOT⁡ρ(α,β)≤CW1(α,β)2/15.\Wass_2(\alpha,\beta) \leq \operatorname{LOT}_\rho(\alpha,\beta) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{LOT}_\rho(\alpha,\beta) \leq C\Wass_1(\alpha,\beta)^{2/15}.W2​(α,β)≤LOTρ​(α,β)andLOTρ​(α,β)≤CW1​(α,β)2/15.
(91)
Proof

The first inequality is immediate: (Tα,Tβ)♯ρ(T_\alpha,T_\beta)_\sharp\rho(Tα​,Tβ​)♯​ρ is a feasible coupling between α\alphaα and β\betaβ. The second inequality is the global quantitative stability theorem of Mérigot, Delalande and Chazal Mérigot et al., 2020. Its proof controls the difference of Kantorovich potentials by W1\Wass_1W1​ and then uses convexity and interpolation estimates to control their gradients in L2(ρ)L^2(\rho)L2(ρ).

In one dimension, quantiles make the embedding isometric and the exponent improves to one. In several dimensions the theorem is global but only Hölder; it is not a global Lipschitz estimate in W2\Wass_2W2​.

Spectral and Robust Wasserstein Distances¶

Spectral OT changes the scalar quadratic cost by measuring the whole displacement covariance through a matrix gauge. The same object admits a robust projected formulation: instead of fixing one projection, one maximizes over the polar set of the gauge. Subspace robust OT is the important non-convex rank-constrained version of this idea Paty & Cuturi, 2019; spectral gauges provide its convex minimax counterpart and connect to recent spectral-gradient viewpoints such as Muon dynamics Peyré, 2026.

Definition: Monotone Spectral Gauge

A monotone spectral gauge on positive semidefinite matrices is a convex, positively 1-homogeneous map γ:S+d→R+\gamma:\mathbb S_+^d\to\RR_+γ:S+d​→R+​ such that γ(M)=0\gamma(M)=0γ(M)=0 only for M=0M=0M=0, γ(QMQ⊤)=γ(M)\gamma(QMQ^\top)=\gamma(M)γ(QMQ⊤)=γ(M) for every orthogonal matrix QQQ, and

0⪯M⪯N⟹γ(M)≤γ(N).0\preceq M\preceq N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \gamma(M)\leq\gamma(N).0⪯M⪯N⟹γ(M)≤γ(N).
(92)

The monotonicity condition means that increasing the displacement covariance in Loewner order cannot decrease the transport penalty.

Definition: Spectral Wasserstein Distance

Let γ\gammaγ be a monotone spectral gauge. For a coupling π∈Π(α,β)\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)π∈Π(α,β), define its displacement covariance

Mπ:=∫(x−y)(x−y)⊤ dπ(x,y).M_\pi \eqdef \int (x-y)(x-y)^\top\d\pi(x,y).Mπ​:=∫(x−y)(x−y)⊤dπ(x,y).
(93)

The spectral Wasserstein distance associated with γ\gammaγ is

Wγ(α,β)2:=inf⁡π∈Π(α,β)γ(Mπ).\Wass_\gamma(\alpha,\beta)^2 \eqdef \inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \gamma(M_\pi).Wγ​(α,β)2:=π∈Π(α,β)inf​γ(Mπ​).
(94)

The special case γ(M)=tr⁡(M)\gamma(M)=\tr(M)γ(M)=tr(M) gives the usual quadratic Wasserstein distance W2\Wass_2W2​. The spectral gauge γ(M)=λmax⁡(M)\gamma(M)=\lambda_{\max}(M)γ(M)=λmax​(M) instead measures the worst transported variance direction. For A⪰0A\succeq0A⪰0, define the quadratic projected transport cost

W2,A(α,β)2:=inf⁡π∈Π(α,β)∫(x−y)⊤A(x−y) dπ(x,y)=W2((A1/2)♯α,(A1/2)♯β)2.\Wass_{2,A}(\alpha,\beta)^2 \eqdef \inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \int (x-y)^\top A(x-y)\d\pi(x,y) = \Wass_2((A^{1/2})_\sharp\alpha,(A^{1/2})_\sharp\beta)^2.W2,A​(α,β)2:=π∈Π(α,β)inf​∫(x−y)⊤A(x−y)dπ(x,y)=W2​((A1/2)♯​α,(A1/2)♯​β)2.
(95)

The equality remains valid when AAA is singular. Projecting any coupling gives one inequality; conversely, disintegrate α\alphaα and β\betaβ over their A1/2A^{1/2}A1/2-images and lift an optimal projected coupling by conditionally coupling the fibers.

The polar set of the gauge is

Bγ:={A⪰0:tr⁡(AM)≤γ(M) for all M⪰0},\mathcal B_\gamma \eqdef \{A\succeq0: \tr(AM)\leq\gamma(M)\ \text{for all } M\succeq0\},Bγ​:={A⪰0:tr(AM)≤γ(M) for all M⪰0},
(96)

so that, for a closed gauge, γ(M)=sup⁡A∈Bγtr⁡(AM)\gamma(M)=\sup_{A\in\mathcal B_\gamma}\tr(AM)γ(M)=supA∈Bγ​​tr(AM).

Assume, for simplicity, that the measures are compactly supported and that γ\gammaγ is closed and finite on the positive semidefinite cone. Then

Wγ(α,β)2=sup⁡A∈BγW2,A(α,β)2.\Wass_\gamma(\alpha,\beta)^2 = \sup_{A\in\mathcal B_\gamma} \Wass_{2,A}(\alpha,\beta)^2.Wγ​(α,β)2=A∈Bγ​sup​W2,A​(α,β)2.

atr⁡(M)≤γ(M)≤btr⁡(M)(M⪰0),a\tr(M)\leq\gamma(M)\leq b\tr(M) \qquad (M\succeq0),atr(M)≤γ(M)≤btr(M)(M⪰0),

In particular, Wγ\Wass_\gammaWγ​ is a distance. When γ\gammaγ is the restriction of a norm to the positive semidefinite cone, finite-dimensional norm equivalence supplies such constants automatically.

Wγ(α,β)2=inf⁡π∈Π(α,β)sup⁡A∈Bγtr⁡(AMπ).\Wass_\gamma(\alpha,\beta)^2 = \inf_{\pi\in\Couplings(\alpha,\beta)} \sup_{A\in\mathcal B_\gamma} \tr(AM_\pi).Wγ​(α,β)2=π∈Π(α,β)inf​A∈Bγ​sup​tr(AMπ​).

aW2(α,β)2≤Wγ(α,β)2≤bW2(α,β)2,a\Wass_2(\alpha,\beta)^2 \leq \Wass_\gamma(\alpha,\beta)^2 \leq b\Wass_2(\alpha,\beta)^2,aW2​(α,β)2≤Wγ​(α,β)2≤bW2​(α,β)2,

Definition: Subspace Robust Wasserstein

For 1≤k≤d1\leq k\leq d1≤k≤d, the Paty--Cuturi subspace robust Wasserstein distance is

SRW⁡2,k(α,β):=sup⁡U⊤U=IkW2((U⊤)♯α,(U⊤)♯β)=sup⁡P2=P=P⊤, tr⁡(P)=kW2,P(α,β).\operatorname{SRW}_{2,k}(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \sup_{U^\top U=I_k} \Wass_2((U^\top)_\sharp\alpha,(U^\top)_\sharp\beta) = \sup_{P^2=P=P^\top,\ \tr(P)=k} \Wass_{2,P}(\alpha,\beta).SRW2,k​(α,β):=U⊤U=Ik​sup​W2​((U⊤)♯​α,(U⊤)♯​β)=P2=P=P⊤, tr(P)=ksup​W2,P​(α,β).

γk(M)=∑ℓ=1kλℓ(M),\gamma_k(M)=\sum_{\ell=1}^k\lambda_\ell(M),γk​(M)=ℓ=1∑k​λℓ​(M),

Trace and spectral gauges for displacement covariances. The trace gauge minimizes the average squared displacement and gives the usual quadratic transport plan. The λmax⁡\lambda_{\max}λmax​ gauge penalizes the worst projected displacement variance; the displayed plan is obtained by approximating the robust formulation with finitely many directions.

The interactive demo turns the displacement covariance into a visible object. The trace gauge sums both covariance eigenvalues, while the top-eigenvalue gauge cares only about the worst transported direction.

Conditional Wasserstein Distances¶

Many applications compare probability laws while keeping an external condition fixed: a class label, a time variable, a spatial location, or, later in Section Conditional Wasserstein Training of Infinite ResNets, the depth of a residual network. The resulting geometry is a fiberwise, or conditional, version of optimal transport. It is based on disintegration of measures and is closely related to conditional and constrained variants of transport used in weak transport and conditional simulation Villani, 2009Santambrogio, 2015Backhoff Veraguas et al., 2019Oliver, 2014Barboni et al., 2024.

The recent literature uses this same fiberwise constraint in several complementary directions. Peszek and Poyato study heterogeneous gradient flows in the topology of fibered optimal transport, emphasizing fixed-fiber transport and PDEs with heterogeneities Peszek & Poyato, 2023. Hosseini, Hsu and Taghvaei develop conditional optimal transport on function spaces through triangular maps and Kantorovich relaxations, motivated by amortized Bayesian inference Hosseini et al., 2025. Chemseddine, Hagemann, Steidl and Wald introduce conditional Wasserstein distances for Bayesian inverse problems and OT flow matching, with restricted couplings that compare posterior laws condition by condition Chemseddine et al., 2025. Kerrigan, Migliorini and Smyth give a dynamic conditional OT formulation and use it to build simulation-free conditional flows Kerrigan et al., 2024. The definition below isolates the common geometric core: transport is ordinary within each fiber and forbidden across distinct conditions.

Definition: Conditional Couplings and Conditional OT

Let (S,λ)(S,\lambda)(S,λ) be a standard Borel probability space of conditions and let (Ω,d)(\Omega,\dist)(Ω,d) be a Polish metric space. For p≥1p\geq1p≥1, denote by Pp,λ(S×Ω)\Pp_{p,\lambda}(S\times\Omega)Pp,λ​(S×Ω) the set of probability measures on S×ΩS\times\OmegaS×Ω whose first marginal is λ\lambdaλ and whose disintegration

α( ds, dx)=αs( dx)λ( ds)\alpha(\d s,\d x)=\alpha_s(\d x)\lambda(\d s)α(ds,dx)=αs​(dx)λ(ds)
(108)

satisfies ∫S∫Ωd(x,x0)p  dαs(x) dλ(s)<+∞\int_S\int_\Omega \dist(x,x_0)^p\,\d\alpha_s(x)\d\lambda(s)<+\infty∫S​∫Ω​d(x,x0​)pdαs​(x)dλ(s)<+∞ for some, hence every, x0∈Ωx_0\in\Omegax0​∈Ω.

For α,β∈Pp,λ(S×Ω)\alpha,\beta\in\Pp_{p,\lambda}(S\times\Omega)α,β∈Pp,λ​(S×Ω), a conditional coupling is a measure

Π( ds, dx, dy)=πs( dx, dy)λ( ds)\Pi(\d s,\d x,\d y) = \pi_s(\d x,\d y)\lambda(\d s)Π(ds,dx,dy)=πs​(dx,dy)λ(ds)
(109)

such that πs∈Π(αs,βs)\pi_s\in\Couplings(\alpha_s,\beta_s)πs​∈Π(αs​,βs​) for λ\lambdaλ-a.e. sss. The set of such couplings is denoted Πλ(α,β)\Couplings_\lambda(\alpha,\beta)Πλ​(α,β). Let (s,x,y)↦cs(x,y)(s,x,y)\mapsto c_s(x,y)(s,x,y)↦cs​(x,y) be jointly Borel, nonnegative, and lower semicontinuous in (x,y)(x,y)(x,y) for every sss. The conditional OT value is

Lcλ(α,β):=inf⁡Π∈Πλ(α,β)∫S∫Ω×Ωcs(x,y) dπs(x,y) dλ(s)=∫Sinf⁡πs∈Π(αs,βs)∫Ω×Ωcs(x,y) dπs(x,y) dλ(s).\begin{aligned} \MK_c^\lambda(\alpha,\beta) &\eqdef \inf_{\Pi\in\Couplings_\lambda(\alpha,\beta)} \int_S\int_{\Omega\times\Omega} c_s(x,y)\d\pi_s(x,y)\d\lambda(s) \\ &= \int_S \inf_{\pi_s\in\Couplings(\alpha_s,\beta_s)} \int_{\Omega\times\Omega} c_s(x,y)\d\pi_s(x,y) \d\lambda(s). \end{aligned}Lcλ​(α,β)​:=Π∈Πλ​(α,β)inf​∫S​∫Ω×Ω​cs​(x,y)dπs​(x,y)dλ(s)=∫S​πs​∈Π(αs​,βs​)inf​∫Ω×Ω​cs​(x,y)dπs​(x,y)dλ(s).​
(110)

The equality in (110) is not a formal exchange of an infimum and an integral. The stated hypotheses make the fiberwise value measurable and permit measurable selection of optimal plans, or measurable near-optimal selection when minimizers are unavailable. Equivalently, conditional transport is ordinary transport on S×ΩS\times\OmegaS×Ω with an infinite cost for moving mass between different values of sss.

Definition: Conditional Wasserstein Distance

For cs(x,y)=d(x,y)pc_s(x,y)=\dist(x,y)^pcs​(x,y)=d(x,y)p, define

Wp,λ(α,β):=(∫SWpp(αs,βs) dλ(s))1/p.\Wass_{p,\lambda}(\alpha,\beta) \eqdef \left( \int_S \Wass_p^p(\alpha_s,\beta_s)\d\lambda(s) \right)^{1/p}.Wp,λ​(α,β):=(∫S​Wpp​(αs​,βs​)dλ(s))1/p.
(111)
Proposition: Metric Property

For p≥1p\geq1p≥1, Wp,λ\Wass_{p,\lambda}Wp,λ​ is a distance on Pp,λ(S×Ω)\Pp_{p,\lambda}(S\times\Omega)Pp,λ​(S×Ω). This metric space is Polish.

Proof

Non-negativity and symmetry follow from the corresponding properties of Wp\Wass_pWp​ on each fiber. If Wp,λ(α,β)=0\Wass_{p,\lambda}(\alpha,\beta)=0Wp,λ​(α,β)=0, then Wp(αs,βs)=0\Wass_p(\alpha_s,\beta_s)=0Wp​(αs​,βs​)=0 for λ\lambdaλ-a.e. sss, hence αs=βs\alpha_s=\beta_sαs​=βs​ for λ\lambdaλ-a.e. sss and the disintegrated measures α\alphaα and β\betaβ coincide. For the triangle inequality, let γ∈Pp,λ(S×Ω)\gamma\in\Pp_{p,\lambda}(S\times\Omega)γ∈Pp,λ​(S×Ω). Since Wp(αs,γs)≤Wp(αs,βs)+Wp(βs,γs)\Wass_p(\alpha_s,\gamma_s)\leq\Wass_p(\alpha_s,\beta_s)+\Wass_p(\beta_s,\gamma_s)Wp​(αs​,γs​)≤Wp​(αs​,βs​)+Wp​(βs​,γs​) for a.e. sss, Minkowski’s inequality in Lp(S,λ)L^p(S,\lambda)Lp(S,λ) gives

Wp,λ(α,γ)≤Wp,λ(α,β)+Wp,λ(β,γ).\Wass_{p,\lambda}(\alpha,\gamma) \leq \Wass_{p,\lambda}(\alpha,\beta)+\Wass_{p,\lambda}(\beta,\gamma).Wp,λ​(α,γ)≤Wp,λ​(α,β)+Wp,λ​(β,γ).
(112)

For completeness and separability, identify each measure with the λ\lambdaλ-a.e. equivalence class of the measurable map s↦αs∈Pp(Ω)s\mapsto\alpha_s\in\mathcal P_p(\Omega)s↦αs​∈Pp​(Ω). The conditional distance is exactly the metric of Lp(S,λ;Pp(Ω))L^p(S,\lambda;\mathcal P_p(\Omega))Lp(S,λ;Pp​(Ω)). Since (Pp(Ω),Wp)(\mathcal P_p(\Omega),\Wass_p)(Pp​(Ω),Wp​) is Polish, so is this metric-valued LpL^pLp space.

Proposition: Conditional Geodesics

Assume that (Ω,d)(\Omega,\dist)(Ω,d) is a geodesic Polish space and let α0,α1∈Pp,λ(S×Ω)\alpha_0,\alpha_1\in\Pp_{p,\lambda}(S\times\Omega)α0​,α1​∈Pp,λ​(S×Ω). For λ\lambdaλ-a.e. sss, choose a constant-speed Wp\Wass_pWp​ geodesic t↦αt,st\mapsto\alpha_{t,s}t↦αt,s​ between α0,s\alpha_{0,s}α0,s​ and α1,s\alpha_{1,s}α1,s​, measurably in sss, and set

αt( ds, dx)=αt,s( dx)λ( ds).\alpha_t(\d s,\d x)=\alpha_{t,s}(\d x)\lambda(\d s).αt​(ds,dx)=αt,s​(dx)λ(ds).
(113)

Then t↦αtt\mapsto\alpha_tt↦αt​ is a constant-speed geodesic for Wp,λ\Wass_{p,\lambda}Wp,λ​.

Proof

For 0≤r≤t≤10\leq r\leq t\leq10≤r≤t≤1, the fiberwise geodesic property gives

Wp(αr,s,αt,s)=(t−r)Wp(α0,s,α1,s)for λ-a.e. s.\Wass_p(\alpha_{r,s},\alpha_{t,s}) = (t-r)\Wass_p(\alpha_{0,s},\alpha_{1,s}) \quad\text{for }\lambda\text{-a.e. }s.Wp​(αr,s​,αt,s​)=(t−r)Wp​(α0,s​,α1,s​)for λ-a.e. s.
(114)

Integrating the pppth power over SSS gives

Wp,λ(αr,αt)=(t−r)Wp,λ(α0,α1).\Wass_{p,\lambda}(\alpha_r,\alpha_t) = (t-r)\Wass_{p,\lambda}(\alpha_0,\alpha_1).Wp,λ​(αr​,αt​)=(t−r)Wp,λ​(α0​,α1​).
(115)

Hence the conditional curve has constant speed and realizes the distance between its endpoints. In Euclidean space one may take, for each sss, an optimal plan πs∈Π(α0,s,α1,s)\pi_s\in\Couplings(\alpha_{0,s},\alpha_{1,s})πs​∈Π(α0,s​,α1,s​) and set αt,s=((1−t)p1+tp2)♯πs\alpha_{t,s}=((1-t)\mathrm p_1+t\mathrm p_2)_\sharp\pi_sαt,s​=((1−t)p1​+tp2​)♯​πs​, where p1,p2\mathrm p_1,\mathrm p_2p1​,p2​ are the two coordinate projections. On a general geodesic space, the same construction uses a measurable family of optimal dynamical plans; when geodesics are non-unique, different measurable selections can produce different conditional geodesics.
